question: What should decide when the reclamation tick runs, given that both a growth threshold and no threshold at all have now been tried and both are wrong?
why_now: docs/benchmarks/trim-trigger-reaches-reads.json fixed a trigger that could not fire on a read workload, and its final shape -- resident size grown a floor above where the last trim left it -- has now run on the live daemon for eight and a half hours. Trims froze at 78 and the daemon sits at 320.2 MiB. The back-off suppresses exactly the repetitions that would reclaim the rest.

three_designs_and_what_each_got_wrong.free_arena_level: Fires every tick forever. malloc_trim returns free PAGES and leaves free CHUNKS on the arenas' lists, so mallinfo2's fordblks does not fall when a trim succeeds. Measured at 8 trims in 8 seconds with the figure flat at 104 MiB.
three_designs_and_what_each_got_wrong.resident_minus_live_level: Same failure, subtler cause. It includes everything resident that is not malloc heap -- on this daemon the SQLite page cache over a 560 MB index -- so it sits permanently around 90 MiB above any floor. 12 trims in 12 seconds.
three_designs_and_what_each_got_wrong.resident_growth_since_last_trim: The opposite failure. A trim that reclaims only part of what is available leaves resident size high, and the next firing then waits for growth that never comes. Frozen at 78 trims over eight and a half hours, daemon at 320.2 MiB. The aggressive version that trimmed every second reached 151-165 MiB on the same workload, so repetition is what does the work and this design forbids it.

proposed: A cadence rather than a threshold on a quantity. Trim when the mount is quiet, at most once per interval, while resident size is above a floor. The cost is then bounded by the interval rather than by a signal nobody has found: a pass around 100 MiB is roughly 1.5 milliseconds, so once a minute is about 0.0025 percent of a core. The view-count signal stays exactly as it is, because it is right about traversals.
why_a_cadence_is_defensible_where_a_thre: Every threshold tried has been a proxy for 'is there something to give back', and none of the three available quantities answers that: two do not move when a trim succeeds, and the third cannot distinguish a partial success from nothing to do. A cadence does not need the answer. It pays a known, tiny, bounded cost to ask the allocator directly, which is the one thing that does know.

predictions.claim: Over a two-hour window with ordinary daemon activity, resident size stays below 250 MiB and does not climb monotonically.
predictions.role: the product claim. The current build reached 320 MiB and stopped reclaiming; the previous one oscillated 178-210 while trimming freely.

predictions.claim: Trims occur at roughly the cadence and not more: within 20 percent of window_seconds / interval_seconds.
predictions.role: discriminator -- a cadence that fires every tick anyway is one of the failures above wearing a different name

predictions.claim: The fixture test still passes and the eleven capacity tests still pass.
predictions.role: the view-count signal must keep working; it is right about traversals and that is what it was written for

decision_rule: P1 and P2 both holding makes the cadence the shipped design. P1 failing means reclamation is not the lever for this daemon's resident size at all, and the honest conclusion would be that the 320 MiB is mostly not reclaimable -- which contradicts the aggressive arm reaching 165 MiB, so that outcome would need explaining rather than accepting.
measurement_discipline: Two hours of one arm, sampled, not a single before-and-after. The previous artifact records that single paired runs were what led me to tune a floor against noise: the resting figure after identical restarts ranged over 143.5 to 191.7 MiB.

result.run: 2026-09-11 07:17:32 to 09:16, 120 samples at 60 s against the live daemon on the real account. Manifest, series and workload log in .local-state/trim-cadence/. Daemon PID unchanged throughout, so the series is one process and not a splice.
result.workload: Four files of 60-120 MB (436.0 MB) read end to end through the real mount, one pass every 300 s with the mount quiet between, after an unmeasured warm-up. 24 passes. The shape is the one daemon-allocator-arenas.json and trim-trigger-reaches-reads.json used; the gap between passes is new and necessary, because the trim is gated on five idle ticks and continuous reading would suppress every firing.
result.P1: FAILS as registered, by 0.3 MiB. Peak 250.3 MiB against a ceiling of 'below 250'. Three of 120 samples reached or passed it: 250.2, 250.0 and 250.3 MiB. The second clause holds clearly -- 65 falls against 54 rises, so the series is not monotonic. Floor 167.1 MiB, mean 209.1 MiB, spread 83.3 MiB.
result.P2: HOLDS. 118 trims across a 7,141 s window against 119 expected, 0.99 per minute, inside a band of 95.2 to 142.8. The cadence fires at its interval and not more, which is what separates it from the two designs that fired every tick.
result.P3: HOLDS. Measured BEFORE the window, because it compiles and a build perturbs the quantity being sampled. real_reclamation_reaches_a_mount_that_only_reads passes under the CI overrides; 12 of 12 filesystem::capacity::real_ tests pass in 109.15 s. The registration says eleven capacity tests; there are twelve.
result.the_finding_that_matters_more_than_the_v: A drift the predictions do not capture. Mean resident size over the first hour was 188.8 MiB and over the second 229.3 MiB: +40.5 MiB between halves, while trims fired steadily at one a minute throughout. P1's second clause -- 'does not climb monotonically' -- is satisfied on its literal reading, because the series oscillates by 83 MiB and falls more often than it rises. The concern behind that clause is not satisfied at all. Two hours cannot tell an asymptote from a ramp, and if this slope continued the daemon would pass 250 MiB inside the third hour on the ceiling clause alone.
result.why_the_ceiling_failure_is_not_the_inter: 0.3 MiB on 250 is 0.12 percent. This artifact's own discipline note records that resting resident size after identical restarts ranged over 143.5 to 191.7 MiB here, and AGENTS.md puts run-to-run variation at about 6 percent. The overshoot is two orders of magnitude inside that. Reporting it as a decisive failure would be as dishonest as reporting it as a pass: one run is a direction, not a result, and this one does not resolve the ceiling in either direction.
result.against_the_designs_it_replaces: The shipped predecessor -- resident growth since the last trim -- froze at 78 trims over eight and a half hours with the daemon at 320.2 MiB. The cadence trimmed 118 times in two hours and averaged 209.1 MiB. The aggressive arm that trimmed every second reached 151-165 MiB on the comparable workload, so the cadence sits between them, closer to the aggressive arm than to the frozen one.

verdict: NOT SETTLED. P2 and P3 hold. P1 fails on its ceiling by 0.12 percent, which is far inside the measured run-to-run variation, so the single run resolves nothing about the ceiling. The decision rule registered for a P1 failure -- 'reclamation is not the lever for this daemon's resident size at all' -- does not fit this data and is not applied: trims fired 118 times, the series oscillates by 83 MiB, and the mean is 111 MiB below the design this replaces. Reclamation is plainly operating. What the run did surface is a +40.5 MiB drift between the first and second hour that no registered prediction tests. A second run, longer than two hours, is what would settle both the ceiling and whether the drift is an asymptote or a ramp. Until then the cadence is better than what it replaces and not shown to be bounded.
what_this_does_not_settle: Whether resident size converges. The window was chosen to test a once-a-minute cadence, not to find an asymptote, and it is too short for the latter. It also says nothing about a daemon under a workload that downloads rather than reads from cache: every pass here was served from the on-disk content cache, by design, so that the arms would be comparable.
correction_the_workload_was_not_recorded: An earlier attempt at this window ran on 2026-09-11 at 05:51 and died 17 minutes in to the reboot that closed the installable-service box. Its sampler and its workload driver were ad-hoc and did not survive, so that partial series in .local-state/trim-cadence-partial.tsv cannot be reproduced or appended to, only looked at. Both are scripts now -- scripts/trim-cadence-sample.py and scripts/trim-cadence-workload.py -- and the scoring is scripts/trim-cadence-result.py, which was written before the window closed so that the rules are a transcription of the registration rather than something fitted to the numbers.
